subject: Astronomy & Space
title: Dwarf Galaxies
description: A quick win: understand Dwarf Galaxies.

hook.text: Dwarf galaxies are tiny—some contain only a few thousand stars. But they vastly outnumber large galaxies.

buildup.text: The Milky Way has at least 50 dwarf satellite galaxies orbiting it. Most are invisible to the naked eye.

discovery.text: Segue 2 is one of the faintest galaxies known—just 1,000 stars held together by an enormous amount of dark matter.

twist.text: Dwarf galaxies may be the building blocks of larger ones. The Milky Way grew by devouring smaller dwarfs over billions of years.

climax.text: Studying them reveals how dark matter behaves on small scales—a key test for our cosmological models.

punchline.text: Tiny galaxies, mostly dark matter. The Milky Way ate many to grow.

quiz.question: Why are dwarf galaxies important for understanding dark matter?
options: Their tiny sizes reveal how dark matter behaves at small scales
They contain no dark matter, providing a contrast to study it
They emit dark matter particles that detectors can measure

details.summary: Dwarf galaxies are small galaxies containing a few billion stars or fewer — compared to the Milky Way's hundreds of billions. They're the most numerous galaxy type in the universe, orbiting as satellites of larger galaxies.
details.whyItMatters: Dwarf galaxies test our understanding of dark matter and galaxy formation. Their abundance, distribution, and dark matter content challenge cosmological models and constrain the nature of dark matter.
takeaways: Small galaxies with a few billion stars or fewer
The most numerous galaxy type in the universe

faq.question: How many dwarf galaxies orbit the Milky Way?
faq.answer: Over 60 satellite galaxies have been discovered, most of them dwarfs. Surveys continue to find ultra-faint dwarfs with only a few thousand visible stars but enormous dark matter halos. Models predict many more remain undiscovered, hidden by their extreme faintness.

faq.question: What is the missing satellites problem?
faq.answer: Dark matter simulations predict thousands of dwarf galaxy-sized dark matter clumps around the Milky Way, but we observe only dozens of satellite galaxies. Either many dark matter halos never formed stars (due to reionization heating or feedback), or the simulations overpredict small structures.
